script.title: Two Girls Fool Sherlock Holmes Creator With Cutout Fairies
sentences: Sherlock Holmes's creator once staked his reputation on real fairies.
In 1917, two young cousins in England borrowed a camera to take photos in their garden.
Nine-year-old Frances and sixteen-year-old Elsie returned with images of tiny winged figures.
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle saw the pictures and declared them proof of the supernatural.
Kodak technicians refused to certify them, but Doyle published them in a national magazine anyway.
Decades later, the women finally admitted the truth.
They had used cardboard cutouts copied from a children's book.
Even the master of detective fiction was fooled by two kids with paper.
script.description:
How two cousins in Cottingley fooled Sir Arthur Conan Doyle with simple cardboard cutouts in 1917.
The story behind one of history's most famous photographic hoaxes.

claims_en: In 1917, nine-year-old Frances Griffiths and sixteen-year-old Elsie Wright took photographs in Cottingley, England.
The photographs depicted tiny winged figures.
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle interpreted the photographs as visible evidence of supernatural phenomena.
Kodak technicians declined to issue a certificate of authenticity for the images.
Conan Doyle published the fairy photographs in the December 1920 edition of The Strand Magazine.
In the early 1980s, Elsie and Frances admitted the photographs were faked using cardboard cutouts copied from a children's book.
